## Overview

A kernel from a space to itself, `X → X`, is a Markov chain: applying it again and
again moves a distribution over `X` forward in time. How quickly that distribution
settles is a form of resilience. After a disturbance, a chain that returns quickly to
its stationary distribution is resilient; one that lingers is not.

[ResilienceCore.jl](https://github.com/ecorecipes/ResilienceCore.jl) holds the
resilience metrics of the ecorecipes packages, and its methods accept such a
kernel directly (ADR 0029):

| function | meaning |
|---|---|
| `linearise(k)` | the chain as a ResilienceCore `MarkovKernel` (row-stochastic) |
| `stationary_distribution(k)` | the distribution the chain settles to, as a labelled state |
| `resilience(k)` | `-log |λ₂|`, the asymptotic rate of approach per step |
| `mixing_time(k; ε)` | the first step at which every start is within total variation `ε` |

This vignette applies them to Horn's model of forest succession.

```{julia}
using FiniteKernels
using ResilienceCore: linearise, stationary_distribution, resilience, mixing_time
using Printf
```

## Horn's forest succession

Horn (1975, "Markovian properties of forest succession", in Cody and Diamond, eds.,
*Ecology and Evolution of Communities*, pp. 196–211) treated a forest as a collection of
sites, each held by one canopy tree. When the tree dies, a sapling growing beneath it
takes its place. The chance that each species replaces each other species is estimated
from the saplings found under trees of each species. One generation of the chain is one
canopy replacement.

The four-species table below is the summary for the Institute Woods in Princeton that
textbooks and teaching material commonly reproduce: grey birch, blackgum, red maple and
beech. **It has not been checked against Horn's chapter for this vignette**, so treat the
numbers as illustrative. Each row is the current occupant and each column the species
that replaces it, so every row sums to one.

```{julia}
tree = FiniteAxis(:tree, [:grey_birch, :blackgum, :red_maple, :beech])
P = [0.05 0.36 0.50 0.09
     0.01 0.57 0.25 0.17
     0.00 0.14 0.55 0.31
     0.00 0.01 0.03 0.96]
succession = cpt([tree], tree, P)
```

`cpt` takes the table in the user-facing layout, parent (the current tree) first and
child (its replacement) last. The kernel stores it outputs first (ADR 0002), and
`linearise` transposes it back to the row-stochastic matrix ResilienceCore expects:

```{julia}
linearise(succession).P ≈ P
```

## From a young forest to the stationary one

Start from a stand of grey birch, the pioneer, and apply the chain one generation at a
time:

```{julia}
x = point_mass(FiniteSpace(tree), :grey_birch)
println(rpad("generation", 12), join(rpad.(string.(labels(tree)), 12)))
for g in 0:8
    println(rpad(g, 12), join(rpad.([@sprintf("%.3f", probability(x, s)) for s in labels(tree)], 12)))
    global x = apply(succession, x)
end
```

The stationary distribution is a labelled state on the same space:

```{julia}
climax = stationary_distribution(succession)
for s in labels(tree)
    @printf("%-11s %.3f\n", s, probability(climax, s))
end
```

Beech holds most sites at stationarity, but the earlier species persist at low
frequencies, because a beech site is occasionally taken by another species.

## How resilient is the composition?

The second-largest eigenvalue modulus `|λ₂|` of the chain sets how quickly a
distribution approaches the stationary one. `resilience` reports `-log |λ₂|` per
generation, so a disturbance decays by a factor `e` in `1 / resilience` generations:

```{julia}
r = resilience(succession)
@printf("resilience %.3f per generation; |λ₂| = %.3f; e-folding %.1f generations\n",
        r, exp(-r), 1 / r)
for ε in (0.25, 0.05, 0.01)
    @printf("mixing time to within total variation %.2f: %d generations\n", ε,
            mixing_time(succession; ε))
end
```

## Disturbance as a second kernel

Disturbance is another kernel on the same space, and composing it with the succession
kernel gives a new chain. Suppose that each generation a fraction `d` of sites is
cleared and recolonised by grey birch, whatever stood there:

```{julia}
function clearing(d)
    T = [(1 - d) * (i == j) + d * (j == 1) for i in 1:4, j in 1:4]
    return cpt([tree], tree, T)
end
println(rpad("d", 6), rpad("beech", 8), rpad("grey birch", 12), rpad("resilience", 12), "mixing (ε = 0.05)")
for d in (0.0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2)
    chain = compose_kernel(succession, clearing(d))
    s = stationary_distribution(chain)
    @printf("%-6.2f%-8.3f%-12.3f%-12.3f%d\n", d, probability(s, :beech),
            probability(s, :grey_birch), resilience(chain), mixing_time(chain; ε=0.05))
end
```

The more frequent the clearing, the less beech the stationary forest holds. Clearing also
pulls every site towards the same start, which speeds the approach to the new
stationary distribution, so resilience in this sense rises with disturbance. It measures
how quickly the composition settles, not whether the late-successional forest survives.

## Kernels that are not chains

A kernel between two different spaces has no dynamics: applying it once leaves the
space it started on. Such a kernel raises a `SpaceMismatchError`. Compose it with a
kernel back to the original space first.

```{julia}
light = FiniteAxis(:light, [:sun, :shade])
canopy_light = cpt([tree], light, [0.9 0.1; 0.6 0.4; 0.3 0.7; 0.1 0.9])
try
    resilience(canopy_light)
catch e
    showerror(stdout, e)
end
```
